text: Booking a table is a simple way to make sure there is a seat for you when you arrive. The restaurant writes down your name, the day, the time and how many people are coming. Plans change, so people often ask to move things around. They say "make it eight instead of seven" or "we are five now, not four." Some ask the assistant to select a place on the same road as the cinema, or a cool spot with a garden. Opening hours matter too, so people check "are you open on Sunday?" before they leave home. If the answer is no, they ask for another day.

name: voice_note_finder
does: Finds a voice note you recorded before, so you can hear it again, even a large one that runs for many minutes.
inputs: a word from the note, like a name or a thing such as a chair, and roughly when you made it
people say:
- Where is that recording I made about the new chair?
- Play the voice note from last Tuesday.
- I said something into my phone about Dad's birthday, find it.
- What was that idea I recorded in the car?
- Can you dig up my old audio notes about the garden?

Theo was kneeling in the garden with muddy gloves when his phone buzzed. A peach tree at the back fence had dropped fruit all week, and tonight he saw a strange shape near the gate. He had invited his sister for dinner and did not want any surprises.

"Check cameras," he said to the phone.

The assistant opened the live view from the back camera and showed it on the screen. Theo leaned close. It was only a neighbour's cat sitting on the wall, washing its paw.

"Thanks," Theo said, laughing at himself. The assistant asked if he wanted a message whenever the camera saw movement after dark. Theo said yes, and the assistant switched on motion alerts for the garden camera until the morning. Then he went back to his peaches.

Most cars tell you when the fuel is low, but it helps to know how much the tank takes. In many places fuel is sold by the liter, so people ask how many liters are left or how far they can drive. Tyre pressure is another thing to check, because soft tyres use more fuel. People say "pump them up a little" or "what should the pressure be?" On cold mornings the windscreen can be icy, so drivers wipe it clean or turn on the heater. Some cars have a manual gearbox, and the driver changes gears by hand. If you forget where you parked, you can ask the car app to show the spot on a map.

Bread dough needs time to rise, and that time depends on the room. In a cold kitchen it can take two hours, and in a warm one only one. Bakers often put the bowl in a spot near a south window, where the sun keeps it cozy. Many recipes explain that the dough should double in size before baking. People ask for help with this all the time. They say "set a timer for forty minutes" or "remind me to check the dough." Later they change the oven: "make it a bit hotter" or "bake it ten minutes more." A friend who works at a hotel bakery once told me the same rules apply to a big batch.

A lawn stays neat when the grass is cut often. Many people now have a robot mower that drives around by itself, and they tell it when to start and when to rest. Some ask it to mow just a single strip by the fence. They say "mow the front lawn today" or "skip tomorrow, it is raining." A sprinkler waters the grass early in the morning, and people change how long it runs: "water for ten minutes less" or "turn it off." Edges look tidy when they are trimmed by hand. A child may climb on the mower by mistake, so it is wise to pause it when kids are outside. Even the kitchen microwave beeps more quietly than a mower, so some people schedule mowing for midday.

Clocks show what time it is where you are, but the world has many time zones. When it is noon in London, it can already be dark in Tokyo. People use a clock app to know the time somewhere else before they make a call. A mother might ask, "what time is it in Sydney? I want to call my son." Others say "show me New York next to my clock" or "is it too late to ring Berlin?" When you travel, the phone changes its clock by itself, but you can also ask it to set the time by hand, or to wake you an hour earlier. Clocks also change in spring and autumn, so people say "did the clocks go forward?"

Person: Good morning. I am a retired teacher, and I would like to find a quiet trail for a walk this weekend, because my knees do better on flat ground and I need to be home before dark.
Assistant: That sounds lovely. Which area would you like to walk in?
Person: The hills north of town. My friends will join me, so I need a path that is wide enough for three.
Assistant: Do you want a short trail, or something that takes half a day?
Person: Short, please. About two hours. And will it rain? My ear aches when the weather turns.
Assistant: I can show the weather, but I cannot say how your ear will feel. Saturday looks dry in the hills.
Person: Then Saturday it is. Please make a daily weather note for the hills until then.

Many hobbies run on small plans. A person who paints may decide to finish a picture by the end of february, and a knitter may want a scarf done before winter. Models and drawings take many evenings, so people set a little time each day. They ask an assistant to help with that. They say "remind me to paint at seven" or "move my knitting hour to Sunday." Someone who buys blue yarn or a new brush may ask "add them to my list." If a friend wants to see the work, people say "send a photo to Anna" or "forward my drawing to my brother." The hobby stays fun because the plan is easy to change.

Marisa woke up late with a dry mouth and felt thirsty and a little silly. Last night she had left the hot tub cover half open. She stumbled to the kitchen, cracked an egg into a pan, then remembered the water.

"What is the hot tub temperature right now?" she asked her speaker.

"It is thirty-two degrees," the assistant said. "Last night it was thirty-eight."

"Oh no. Heat it back up to thirty-eight, please."

The assistant turned on the heater and said it would take about two hours. Marisa then asked it to remind her to close the cover once she was done. She also asked it to read the pump's weekly clean list, which had three hundred words on it. The assistant read the first part, and Marisa ate her breakfast and listened.

They want to know how far they rode today.
- Distance?
- How far did I go?
- How many kilometres was my ride this morning?
- My legs feel like jelly, how long was that ride?
- Tell me the length of today's ride from the shelf where I left my phone, I mean from the start to the end.
- I am hungry and I need to know if I earned a big lunch, so how far did I cycle?
- Could you please tell me the total distance of my last ride?
- I want to design a longer route next time, so how far did I get today?
- Please show me the miles for my bike ride.

A workout plan is a list of exercises you do on certain days. Each exercise has sets and reps. A set is one round, and reps are the times you do the move in that round. Many people find it hard to start, and a new gym can make you feel scared. A plan helps because you know what to do. People change plans all the time. They say "add one more set" or "make Friday a rest day" or "find me an easy leg workout." If someone is tired or sore, they ask for "fewer reps" or "a lighter day." Rest days matter, too. Muscles grow when you rest. If you get hurt, go to a hospital or a doctor and do not push through it.

They want to spend less time walking by seeing their steps and checking the pace.
- Steps and pace, please.
- How many steps today, and was I quick?
- Show me my distance and tell me how fast I went.
- My shoes feel loose and I think I walked slowly, so what was my pace and how many steps did I take?
- Can you tell me how far I ran and what my average speed was?
- Give me this week's steps, and also tell me which day was my longest.
- I have a task at noon, so could you please tell me how long my run was and how far I went?
- What is my step count, and how does it compare with yesterday?

Person: Hello? I do not know how this works. I want the radio.
Assistant: Hello! I can help. Which station would you like?
Person: The news one. It is so quiet in here, I need some noise.
Assistant: I can play the news station on your speaker. Is it the local news or the world news?
Person: The local news, please. They say the town may earn a prize this year.
Assistant: Playing the local news now. Is the volume fine?
Person: A little louder. The old vent in the kitchen makes a loud sound and the news is raw and hard to hear.
Assistant: I made the volume louder. Tell me if you want it even higher.

Leila got home after a long night shift at the clinic. The air in her flat felt dry and heavy, and she could see dust floating near the mirror in the hall. She dropped her bag by the door and said, "Turn on the air purifier in the bedroom, please."

The assistant switched it on at a soft speed so it would not wake her neighbour's baby through the thin wall.

"Wait, no, I mean the living room one," Leila said. "I will sleep on the sofa today."

The assistant turned off the bedroom purifier and turned on the one in the living room. Then it asked if she wanted the humidifier too. Leila nodded and said yes, and the assistant switched it on. She lay down, and the room hummed quietly.

Tariq had been in the city for only a week, and his new phone already had a serious problem. The battery was almost empty by lunchtime. He sat on a bench in the yard behind his building and said, "Why is my battery so bad?"

The assistant showed him which apps used the most power. A map app had been open all morning.

"Turn on battery saver," Tariq said.

The assistant did, and the screen got a little dimmer. Tariq then asked it to pair his earbuds, which he had bought at the market. The assistant found them and connected them. Last, Tariq asked for the battery level in a number. "Twenty-five percent," the assistant said, and it offered to remind him to charge the phone when he got home.

A pool needs care to stay clean. A pump moves the water through a filter, and most people let it run for a few hours each day. If the water looks messy, with leaves or green spots, people ask for help. They say "turn the pump on now" or "stop the pump, someone is cleaning." Hot tubs have a heater, so people also say "make it warmer" or "keep it at thirty-eight." When they go on a trip, they ask to pause the schedule and resume it when they are back at home. A cover keeps out the dirt and keeps the heat in, so "remind me to put the cover on" is a common request.

Rest days are part of a good fitness plan. Many people feel busy and want to train every day, but muscles need time to heal. A plan might say train on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and rest on the other days. A tired person might tell the assistant, "skip today's workout" or "move it to tomorrow." If someone starts a run and feels sick, they say "stop the timer" or "end my workout." Others ask for a break in the middle: "pause for a minute." After a long workout, people eat a simple meal, like toast with eggs, and drink water. Some also ask the assistant to remind them to stretch.

They want the score of a match that is on now.
- Score?
- What's the score?
- Who is winning?
- Is it still a draw?
- How did my team do today?
- Could you check the score for me? I left my phone in a small sink of bubbles and I cannot look.
- Tell me what the score is in the football game.
- Can I borrow a minute of your time to hear the latest score from the match?
- Please tell me the result of the game.

A packing list helps you remember what to take on a camping trip. It starts with the big things, like a tent, a sleeping bag and a lamp. Then come small things like socks, a hat and a first aid kit. People like to make a list at home and check each thing off before they leave. They say "add a rain coat" or "take off the extra jacket, it will be warm." Many families cook on a small stove, so they add pots, plates and matches. Some people take a photo of the packed car as a memory. A monthly trip may need a lighter list, so people ask to save the list and use it again.

Freya sat on a box labelled KITCHEN and texted her phone assistant. The new flat had a hard floor and no heater, and the only warm thing was her scarf. She had spent the morning moving boxes up the stairs and now her fingers felt cold.

"brrr, it's like swimming in an icy lake in here," she typed.

The assistant understood and turned the smart heater in the living room up by two degrees. It also said the pizza place nearby had a crispy deal tonight, but she had not asked for that. Freya laughed and typed, "no pizza yet, but thanks."

"Do you want me to remind you at six?" the assistant asked. She typed yes, and a small reminder appeared on the screen.

name: bus_delay_checker
does: Tells you if a bus or train is late and how long the wait will be, even on a stormy day when everything runs slowly.
inputs: the line or route number, and the stop where you are waiting
people say:
- Is the number nine bus late?
- Do you have any idea when the next train comes?
- I have been standing here for twenty minutes, what happened to the bus?
- Is the line to the airport running normally today?
- Will I make my train if I leave in ten minutes?
- Tell me if my tram is delayed. I would hate to pay for a taxi if it is only a short wait.

Abigail stood in the kitchen with a spoon in one hand and her phone in the other. The kids were asking for a film night, and she needed something nice and short. She had only a single free evening this week.

"What films are on at the cinema on the twelfth of March?" she asked.

The assistant listed four films for that day and showed the times. One was a cartoon about a fox that started at five.

"Book two seats for the cartoon," she said, "and a big popcorn if saving some money is possible."

The assistant booked the seats and said the combo deal with popcorn cost less than buying them apart. Abigail said yes, and the assistant sent her the tickets.

Alessandro rolled over, rubbed his eyes and grabbed his phone. The bedroom was grey, and he could not remember if he had paid the water bill. He felt his stomach drop a little. The last one had been very low, so this one should be too, but the due date was close.

"Water bill?" he mumbled.

The assistant said the water bill was one hundred and ten euros and was due on Friday. It had not been paid yet.

"Pay it," said Alessandro.

The assistant asked him to confirm the amount, and he said yes. A moment later it told him the payment was done and a receipt was in his email.

"Thank you," he said, and went to make coffee, feeling much better.

Eleni was unpacking boxes behind the counter of her little shop when the door chime rang. A courier stood there with a big parcel. It was the third one this week. She signed on the screen and then looked at the pile of mail on the desk, with a heap of letters beside a box smelling of fish from the market.

"Track parcel," she said to her phone.

The assistant asked which one. She read the number from a sticker, and the assistant said that parcel had been dropped at the shop an hour ago and was signed for. Then she asked if the total of waiting parcels was right. It said yes: four packages in all. Eleni nodded and cleared the desk for the next one.

A work meeting is easier when everyone knows the plan. The agenda is a short list of what will be talked about, and people send it before the call. To join a call, you click a link or ask your assistant to open it. Some people join from far away, so sound and screen sharing matter. People say "share my screen" or "turn my microphone off" or "make the camera brighter." If a call is running long, they ask to adjust the plan: "move the next item to tomorrow" or "give us five more minutes." Some teams even book a meeting room by the hour, like a pound for each minute, in a joke about how time costs money.

Person: Sun cream.
Assistant: Sure. Do you want me to add it to your shopping list, or are you looking for the weather and UV level?
Person: Shopping list. I own a small shop near the beach and tourists keep asking.
Assistant: Okay. Which kind: for kids, or for adults?
Person: Both, please. And can you convert the temperature of the sea into Fahrenheit? A customer from the US asked me.
Assistant: Today the sea is eighteen degrees Celsius, which is about sixty-four Fahrenheit.
Person: Neat. Also, can you make the swimming flags work from here?
Assistant: I am sorry, I cannot control the beach flags. I can tell you what colour they are today.
Person: That is fine. Thanks.

Person: I want to see more likes on my garden pictures.
Assistant: I cannot make people like your pictures, but I can show how many likes each one has. Do you want that?
Person: Yes. Show me the one with the dream roses first.
Assistant: That post has forty likes. Half of them came yesterday.
Person: Oh, tiny but nice! Post another one tomorrow.
Assistant: Which photo should I post, and at what time?
Person: The tomatoes, at nine in the morning. And no sad face on it, please. My neighbour told me a joke last time and I did not want to cry from laughing.
Assistant: Okay. I will post the tomato photo at nine tomorrow with no sad face.

A calendar keeps your plans in one place. Each event has a day, a start time and an end time, and many have a short note. People use a calendar to see when they are free, and they ask an assistant to add or change things. They say "put dentist on Tuesday at three" or "move my meeting to Thursday." If two events happen at once, the assistant tells them. Some people design their week with colours: blue for work, green for home. A family might share a calendar, with a single page on the fridge at home and the same one on their phones. When a plan is cancelled, people say "delete it" or "take it off."

Person: Quick, how long since the baby ate?
Assistant: Do you mean the last bottle or the last meal?
Person: The bottle. I do not want the long list, just the time.
Assistant: The last bottle was at two o'clock, so about three hours ago.
Person: Good. She is total chaos today. Put her nap on the schedule, please. And she has to wear the warm hat, since it is cold.
Assistant: I can add the nap. What time should it start?
Person: Four. Not five. My son's hamster needs feeding at five.
Assistant: Nap at four, noted. I cannot feed the hamster, but I can remind you at five.
Person: Please do.

They want to find out what is on at the cinema.
- Anything good on?
- What's playing tonight?
- Show me films near me.
- I am so sad and bored, I need a good laugh at the movies.
- There is nothing to do this Thursday, any films showing?
- Could you tell me which films are on at the cinema by the park?
- I want to see something new, what are the new releases?
- If it is not too much trouble, would you please check which movies are showing, as my friends and I need to park nearby and plan the evening?

When you order something online, the shop sends it to your address. You can pick a size, a colour and a day for delivery. Sometimes plans change, and people ask to edit the order. They say "change the size to medium" or "send it to my office instead." If a parcel is left at the gate and not at the door, people say "tell the driver to knock." Some shops let you drop an item off at a shop to return it. If the thing is wrong, people write "sorry, this does not fit" and ask for their money back. An assistant can track the parcel too, and say "it will come tomorrow."

name: packing_helper
does: Keeps a list of moving boxes, what is inside each one, and which room it goes to, so you can find the box with the cool things, like the kettle, fast.
inputs: the box label or number, the things inside, and the room
people say:
- Which box has my plates?
- Where did I put the cables?
- Add the winter coats to box twelve.
- My mom needs the pan, what box is it in?
- Which boxes go to the bedroom?
- Where is the box with the cat's food bowl? The cat needs to be fed.

Ella closed her shop at six and walked to her car. A single light was on in the car park, and the fuel light on her dashboard was glowing. She sat in the driver seat and said, "Hey car, how much fuel do I have?"

The assistant said she had a quarter of a tank, enough for about sixty kilometres.

"Good. Is the tyre pressure okay? I would prefer to know before the long road home."

The assistant checked and told her the front left tyre had less air than the others. It was half a bar low. Ella asked it to find the nearest petrol station with an air pump. The assistant showed one two minutes away on the map and started the directions. She pulled out and kept her mouth closed, listening.

They want to know what homework is due soon.
- Homework due?
- What do I have to hand in this week?
- Tell me which assignments are due on Friday.
- I forgot my diary, can you read out my homework list?
- Is there anything due tomorrow? The weather is stormy and I do not want to go out and find out.
- I need to finish thirty-one pages of reading, which subject was that for?
- Please ask the speaker to tell me what is due before the end of the week.
- Could you please tell me my deadlines for maths and history?

It was a rainy afternoon, and Lars came in from the garden with mud all over his boots. The floor in the hall looked terrible. He had forgotten that guests were coming for tea.

"Start the robot vacuum in the hall," he said, "in twenty minutes."

The assistant set a timer. Then Lars looked at his cleaning schedule on the screen and said, "Pull up the schedule for the week." The assistant showed it. The vacuum usually ran on Monday and Thursday mornings.

Lars took off his boots and asked the assistant to mop the hall on Saturday as well. It added the task. Twenty minutes later the little vacuum hummed to life and rolled across the muddy spots, and Lars sat down with his tea.

Kasia was behind the counter of her flower shop when her phone rang with a call reminder. A meeting with her supplier was about to begin, and she had left the link in her inbox. Her hands were full of ribbon, so she typed fast.

"join the evnt with marek now"

The assistant understood and opened the meeting on her phone. The screen showed her supplier's face. Kasia propped the phone against a vase and carried on with the ribbon.

A few minutes later she said, "play the agenda," and the assistant read it out loud. There was less to discuss than she had feared: prices, one late delivery and a new type of rose. When the call ended, the assistant asked if she wanted notes sent to her email, and she said yes.

Leticia did not like technology, but her daughter had put a smart speaker in the living room. Today she was planning a short trip to a little village by the sea, and she wanted a hotel.

"Um, hello? I want to book a room for three nights," she said slowly.

The assistant asked which dates, and Leticia gave them. It found a small hotel with a free breakfast and read out the price.

"Oh, wait, I made a mistake. Two nights, not three. My husband cannot come for the last one."

The assistant changed the booking to two nights and said the room was for two guests. It asked if she wanted it to boil down the choices by showing only rooms with a sea view. She said yes, thank you, and it did.

Board games are more fun when everyone agrees on the rules. People use a timer to keep each turn short and a score sheet to see who is ahead. At the end of a game, someone counts the points and says who won. Players often ask a smart speaker for help: "set a one minute timer" or "add ten points for Ben." If a player makes a mistake, they say "take two points off" or "start the round again." A game can feel long, and by the middle everyone wants a snack. If you are keeping a receipt from the shop for a new game, you may need it for a return. Puzzles are quieter, and people use a timer to see how fast they finish.

Edward was eight, and he wanted to bake bread with his grandma. She had gone to the shop for butter, so he stood by the oven and asked the speaker, "How long does bread take to bake?"

"About thirty minutes at two hundred degrees," the assistant said.

"Okay. Put the oven on, but not too hot. I do not want it to burn."

The assistant said it could only set the temperature if he asked it to, so he said, "Two hundred." The oven began to get warm. Edward did not want to rush, so he asked for a timer for thirty minutes. When his grandma came home, the kitchen smelled lovely, and they both waited for the warm loaf to come out.

Niamh finished her night shift at seven and wanted a slow walk home to wake up. The morning was chilly, and her feet hurt. She asked her phone, "Start a walk, and track the distance."

The assistant began recording. After ten minutes, Niamh stopped by a bench and said, "Actually, no, I mean a run. A slow one. I need to burn off this coffee."

The assistant changed the activity from walking to running and kept the minutes so far. It asked if she wanted it to notify her at each kilometre. Niamh said yes.

At the first kilometre the watch buzzed, and a calm voice told her the pace. She smiled. Then she remembered a small loan she owed a friend and asked the assistant to remind her about it that evening.

They want to make the text bigger and also see how many words they have written.
- Bigger text and a word count, please.
- Can you zoom in on my page and tell me how many words there are?
- The letters look tiny, and I want to know if I reached five hundred words.
- Increase the font size and show me my word count.
- I am working in a bad light from a bulb that is too dim, can you make the text larger and count my words too?
- Make this bigger, and then check the spelling.
- Please make the writing easier to read and tell me how long my story is. It is taking a bitter long time to finish.
- Larger text, word count, thanks.

Emre had taught history for thirty years, and he loved to eat out. This Friday he wanted a quiet dinner for two. He sat on his sofa with a bar of soap on the table, since he had just washed his hands, and said to the speaker, "Find me an Italian restaurant that is open tonight."

The assistant gave him three names. Emre said, "Not the one on the main street, it is too loud. I do not want to wait outside either."

The assistant took that place off the list and called the second restaurant to ask about a table. It said a table was free at eight. "That is fine," said Emre. The assistant booked it for two and sent him the address.

Shirin was a student with an exam in two weeks, and her group chat would not stop beeping. She was cooking dinner and frying onions in a pan, and the phone sat on the shelf, inside a plastic bag to keep the grease off.

"Read my new messages," she said.

The assistant read three messages. One from Dara said the study group would meet at the library on Sunday.

"Reply, I will be there at ten," said Shirin.

The assistant sent the reply. Then Shirin said, "And remind me in two weeks to send Dara my thanks for the notes." The assistant set the reminder, and Shirin turned back to the glue of onions sticking to the pan and stirred them.

They want a note to be saved without the whole thing being read out.
- Save this note, but do not read it back.
- Just write down my idea, no reply needed.
- Do not make a long note, only the main point.
- I do not want a voice message, please type it.
- My bag is heavy and my hands are full, so jot this down and do not ask me questions.
- When the bus arrives, write down what I say, but no beeping sound.
- Keep it short, and do not send a link to anyone.
- Could you please save this thought for me and not open the notes app until I ask?

Rafaela was nine, and it was her turn to help her mum shop for school things. They were in the living room with the tablet on the table. Her old shoes had a hole in the bottom, and march was only a week away.

"Find me new school shoes," Rafaela told the assistant.

The assistant showed some. She picked a pair and asked, "Do you have these in a size bigger? My feet are growing."

The assistant said they did and that they cost half as much as the shoes in the other shop. Rafaela clapped. Her phone buzzed to say the order could arrive the next day, and she asked it to put the order in. Then she asked for double socks, and the assistant added two packs to the basket.

name: burn_care_guide
does: Tells you the first steps to take for a small burn, and says when it is time to call for help, so you do not need to lift a hand to a pricey doctor for every little thing.
inputs: where the burn is, how big it is, and what caused it
people say:
- I touched the hot pan, what do I do?
- My arm is red after the oven, should I put ice on it?
- How do I treat a burn from boiling water?
- When should a burn go to the doctor?
- My driver friend burnt his hand on the car engine, help.
- Is a blister on my finger serious?

Layla was standing outside the cinema with her friends, and the night was cold. The streets were quiet, and there was only a television playing in a shop window across the road. Her hands felt like ice.

She texted her phone assistant, "my feet are freezing and i dont want to jog home lol."

The assistant understood that she needed a ride. It asked, "Do you want me to book a taxi from here?"

"Yes please."

It found a car three minutes away and showed the driver's name and the plate. It asked if the pickup point was the front door of the cinema, and Layla said yes. The assistant sent a message when the car arrived, and Layla and her friends climbed in, glad of the heater.

Bo was on the sofa with a baby on one knee and a laptop on the other when the phone rang about the family trip. His son wanted to see the sea, and a temporary break from work sounded perfect.

"Find a hotel by the beach for fifteen nights in August," Bo told the assistant, and then he groaned. "No, that is too long. I only have a week."

The assistant said, "I will look for seven nights." It showed a family room that would last the whole week and cost a fair price. Bo asked if breakfast was included, and the assistant said yes, and also that check-in was at three.

Bo asked it to book the room for two adults and one child, and it sent him the details.

They want the phone to read the text on the screen out loud.
- Read this aloud.
- Read it to me.
- Can you speak the words on my screen?
- The letters are blurry today, please read the page.
- I want to hear this article instead of reading it.
- Please read my monthly email, I left my glasses in the vinegar cupboard, where I hide them from the kids.
- Would you please read the text out loud for me? My eyes get tired in the evening, and listening is much easier than looking at a small screen.
- Start reading from the top and go slowly.
